Haemolysis frequency compared for the 1-year period before (22-, 23-, 25-gauge; 155,318 serum samples) vs after (23- and 25-gauge only; 149,963 serum samples). A diagnostic support system selected 90 outpatients (>18 y, eGFR >=45) with HI 0-1 in the 90 days before the needle change and HI >=2 within 90 days after. Haemolysis frequency rose after the change: HI>=1 3.50% -> 4.29% (RR 1.23), HI>=2 0.625% -> 1.00% (RR 1.61), HI>=4 0.0985% -> 0.283% (RR 2.88), all p<0.001. Study method details: Prospective comparative study, May 2018 - July 2019; 211 patients aged >=18 admitted with a 20G/22G peripheral venous catheter (PVC) inserted within the last 24 h; 237 blood tests. Paired sampling: a morning direct venipuncture stab (DVS) sample, then a second sample drawn from the PVC within 10 minutes. PVC protocol: flushed with 2 mL saline, 20-second wait, vein blocked for 15 seconds, 5-mL syringe attached, a 5-mL 'dead space' sample discarded, then blood drawn into tubes with controlled syringe aspiration; PVC washed again with 2 mL saline. Agreement assessed by intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), Bland-Altman 95% agreement interval (AI) and a clinically accepted interval (CAI).
Additional sources of bias: Single-centre, single-department study (stated limitation); sample power calculated only for the primary outcome, so statistical strength is reduced for secondary outcomes; the PVC-drawn samples had a significantly higher total haemolysis rate than DVS on day 1 (10.9% vs 1.47%, P=.002), which is the mechanism by which K would be biased, yet no potassium concentrations are printed
